title: Prompt Engineering is Dead — Nir Gazit, Traceloop
talk_summary: Speaker argues manual prompt engineering is not real engineering; he builds an evaluator with expected facts and an LLM judge, then an agent iteratively rewrites prompts using failure reasons and online guides. He reports a RAG chatbot score rising from 0.4 to 0.9 in two iterations, while warning about overfitting and noting he still had to engineer the optimizer agent.

takeaways.what_they_do: They create questions with expected facts; an LLM judge checks each fact in the generated answer and returns pass/fail plus a reason; the aggregate score is correct facts divided by total facts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for each question, I'm going to write what do I expect the answer to contain
takeaways.numbers: 20 examples x 3 facts = 60 facts; score 0.4 to 0.9 after two iterations; evaluator takes a couple of minutes

takeaways.what_they_do: A researcher agent runs the evaluator, combines failure reasons with prompting guides, generates a new prompt, and repeats while the score improves.
takeaways.evidence_quote: combine the reasons for failures plus prompting guides to get a new prompt

takeaways.what_they_do: They warn that optimizing on all examples overfits; they recommend splitting examples into train and test/eval sets and validating separately.
takeaways.evidence_quote: split it into train test uh sets or train test evo sets

takeaways.what_they_do: They evaluate pipeline steps separately, like retrieval versus final generation, calling it similar to unit testing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can kind of evaluate each step separately. You can evaluate each one

takeaways.what_they_do: The speaker uses an agent to optimize prompts but admits he still had to engineer the optimizer agent; the loop is offline against an evaluator.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I've actually done a lot of prompt engineering for this demo because I needed to engineer the agent
